cards.text: Joshua, Israel's leader, has died (Joshua 24:29), and there are still Canaanites in the land to fight. Somebody has to go first. So the Israelites do the smart thing and ask the LORD who it'll be.

cards.question: The Israelites ask who goes up first against the Canaanites. Which tribe does the LORD pick?
Before a single battle is fought, the LORD says He has already delivered the land into their hands.

cards.text: Judah doesn't go alone, though. The men of Judah turn to their brothers, the Simeonites, with a deal.

cards.question: What deal do the men of Judah offer the Simeonites?

answers.text: Fight with us and we will fight with you
Fight for us and we will pay you well
Guard our land while we go and fight

cards.text: Simeon says yes faster than I say yes to a second batch. Judah attacks at Bezek, and the LORD delivers the Canaanites and Perizzites into their hands.

cards.question: At Bezek, the men of Judah strike down ten thousand men.

cards.text: There at Bezek they find Adoni-bezek, a Canaanite ruler, and fight against him. He runs, and they chase him down and seize him.

cards.question: What do the men of Judah do to Adoni-bezek once they catch him?

answers.text: Cut off his thumbs and big toes
Put out both of his eyes
Shave off half of his beard

cards.text: Then Adoni-bezek speaks up. He says seventy kings with their thumbs and big toes cut off used to gather the scraps under his table.

cards.question: Adoni-bezek did this same thing to seventy kings. So what does he say has happened to him now?

answers.text: God has paid him back for it
Judah is crueler than he ever was
His own gods will avenge him soon

cards.text: Seventy kings, and the man kept COUNT. They bring him to Jerusalem, and he dies there.

cards.question: Next, the men of Judah fight against Jerusalem and ___ it.

cards.text: They put Jerusalem to the sword and set it on fire. And friend, Judah is only just warming up the oven.
Next, Judah marches down to fight the Canaanites in the hill country, the Negev and the foothills. Three fronts at once, and I can't even handle TWO timers going off.

cards.question: Judah marches on Hebron, which used to be called Kiriath-arba. There, they strike down three men named Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai.

cards.text: From there, Judah marches on Debir, which used to be called Kiriath-sepher. Then Caleb, the spy who followed the LORD fully back in Moses' day (Numbers 13:6; 14:24), makes an announcement.

cards.question: What does Caleb promise the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it?
Somebody takes Caleb up on his offer and captures the city. Who is it?

cards.text: One day Acsah urges Othniel to ask her father for a field. When she gets off her donkey, Caleb asks her, “What do you desire?”

cards.question: Acsah answers, “Give me a blessing.” Caleb has already given her land in the Negev. What does she ask him to give her as well?
Caleb gives Acsah only the upper springs.

cards.text: She asked for springs and got the upper AND the lower. Back in the junk drawer I asked for one inch of elbow room, and the drawer just stayed SHUT.
Meanwhile, the descendants of Moses' father-in-law, the Kenite, go up with the men of Judah. They travel from the City of Palms to the Wilderness of Judah, in the Negev near Arad.

cards.question: Once they get there, the Kenites go to live among the people.

cards.text: Then Judah teams up with their brothers the Simeonites again. They attack the Canaanites living in Zephath and devote the city to destruction.

cards.question: After that, the city of Zephath gets a new name. What is it called?

cards.text: Judah also captures Gaza, Ashkelon and Ekron, each with its territory. The LORD is with Judah, and they take the hill country, but the plains are another story.

cards.question: Judah can't drive out the people living in the plains, because those people have chariots of ___.

cards.text: And just as Moses had promised, Judah gives Hebron to Caleb. Moses made that promise way back, and here it is, delivered fresh out of the oven.

cards.question: In Hebron, Caleb drives out the descendants of the three sons of Anak.

cards.text: And that's where we'll leave it for now, friend. Trust me, this story is far from done.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 7 quotes "Give me a blessing.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: "Simeon says yes faster than I say yes to a second batch" states two things about the Simeonites that the text never says: that they said yes, and that they agreed quickly. Judges 1:3 says only "So the Simeonites went with them." The joke's comparison should not make a claim about Simeon that the text doesn't support.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: Adoni-bezek is called "a Canaanite ruler." The text never says which people he belonged to. Judges 1:5 names both the Canaanites and the Perizzites. A safer intro would be the ruler or king at Bezek.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: "Three fronts at once" adds a time the text doesn't give. Judges 1:9 says Judah marched against the Canaanites in the hill country, the Negev and the foothills. It never says these happened at the same time. The joke depends on that added claim.

rule.text: Times stay true. No time in the text means none added.

findings.problem: Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai appear for the first time with nothing said about who they are. Numbers 13:22 calls them descendants of Anak. The cards also never connect them to "the three sons of Anak" in card 17.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: Othniel first appears only as the answer to card 5, "Othniel son of Kenaz." No card says who he is: the son of Caleb's younger brother Kenaz. No card says that Caleb gave him Acsah in marriage (Judges 1:13). Card 6 then talks about Acsah and Othniel as if the baker already knows they are married.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: "She asked for springs and got the upper AND the lower" repeats the answer to card 8 and doesn't move the passage forward. Only the joke is new.

rule.text:
Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.
- No recap cards.

findings.problem: The joke invents a new moment in Papa Dorin's backstory: he asked for elbow room in the junk drawer and the drawer stayed shut. The allowance for invented small moments is limited to his bakery. This adds a new event to the drawer story instead.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.

findings.problem: "Meanwhile" says the Kenites' move happened at the same time as the events before it. Judges 1:16 opens with "Now" and doesn't say how the two connect in time.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The card packs in more than two beats: Judah captures Gaza, Ashkelon and Ekron (1:18); the LORD is with Judah and they take the hill country (1:19); and a setup tease about the plains. It should be split.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: The story-isn't-over line nearly copies the doc's example word for word: "And that's where we'll leave it for now, friend. Trust me, this story is far from done."

rule.text: The examples show the idea. Write your own line each time.

findings.problem: The humor is thin. Most lines read as pleasant rather than laugh-out-loud funny. Stop 2 cards 2 through 8 have no humor at all. Several jokes are mild oven puns: stop 1 card 14 "only just warming up the oven," and stop 2 card 16 "delivered fresh out of the oven." The second sentence of stop 2 card 16 mostly restates the first.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: Five of the six true or false cards have True as the answer: stop 1 cards 3 and 7, and stop 2 cards 2, 11 and 17. Only stop 2 card 8 is False. Several of the True cards are bare restatements of a fact the baker has no way to reason about, such as stop 2 card 2 with Hebron and the three names. A baker can learn that "True" is almost always right, which turns these cards into luck or a pattern rather than an informed guess.
findings.question: Should the docs require true or false answers to be balanced across a stop or a walkthrough, or limit true or false cards whose statement is a new fact the baker can't reason about?
